Pregnancy

The First Trimester: A Week-by-Week Guide to Weeks 1–12

Updated: July 1, 2026

The first trimester covers weeks 1 through 12 and is a time of remarkable, mostly invisible change. Your baby develops from a single cell into a tiny form with a beating heart and the beginnings of every major organ, while your body adjusts through a surge of hormones. This guide walks through what is happening, how you might feel, and the simple steps that support a healthy start.

What is happening to your baby

Pregnancy is dated from the first day of your last menstrual period, so the first couple of weeks technically happen before conception. After fertilization, the embryo implants in the uterus and begins to grow quickly.

By around week 6 a heartbeat can often be detected, and by the end of week 12 the major organs, limbs, fingers, and toes have formed. Your baby is roughly the size of a lime and is now called a fetus.

Common early symptoms

Rising hormones drive most early symptoms: nausea (the misnamed "morning sickness" that can strike any time of day), tender breasts, fatigue, frequent urination, food aversions, heightened smell, and mood changes.

Symptoms vary enormously — some people feel very unwell, others barely notice anything, and both can be perfectly normal. Most nausea eases as the second trimester begins.

Small, frequent meals, staying hydrated, gentle snacks like crackers, and rest can take the edge off the most common discomforts.

Nutrition and folic acid

A prenatal vitamin with folic acid is one of the most important early steps. Getting enough folic acid before and during early pregnancy significantly lowers the risk of neural tube defects, which form in these first weeks.

Aim for a balanced plate: vegetables and fruit, whole grains, protein, dairy or fortified alternatives, and iron- and calcium-rich foods. You do not need to "eat for two" in the first trimester — quality matters far more than quantity.

What to avoid

Avoid alcohol, smoking, and recreational drugs entirely. Limit caffeine (many guidelines suggest keeping it modest), and skip high-risk foods such as raw or undercooked meat and eggs, unpasteurized dairy, high-mercury fish, and deli meats unless heated.

Check any medications and supplements with your healthcare provider before continuing them, since some are not recommended in pregnancy.

Your first prenatal appointment

Your first prenatal visit is usually one of the most detailed. Expect a review of your health history, an estimated due date, blood and urine tests, and a chance to ask questions. Some clinics offer an early ultrasound to confirm dating.

This is a good time to discuss any existing conditions, medications, family history, and what care schedule to expect through your pregnancy.

Warning signs — when to call your doctor

Contact your provider promptly for heavy vaginal bleeding, severe or one-sided abdominal pain, a high fever, severe vomiting that prevents keeping fluids down, fainting, or severe pain when urinating.

Light spotting and mild cramping can be normal, but when in doubt it is always reasonable to call — your care team would rather answer a question than have you worry alone.

Caring for your mind, too

The first trimester can be an emotional mix of excitement, anxiety, and exhaustion, sometimes before you have even told anyone. That is completely normal.

Rest when you can, lean on your partner or a trusted friend, and reach out to your provider if low mood or anxiety feels persistent. Support early makes a real difference.

Key takeaways

  • The first trimester (weeks 1–12) is when your baby’s major organs form — a critical window.
  • Start a prenatal vitamin with folic acid as early as possible to protect early development.
  • Nausea, fatigue, and tender breasts are common; symptom intensity varies widely and that is normal.
  • Avoid alcohol, smoking, high-risk foods, and unchecked medications.
  • Know the warning signs (heavy bleeding, severe pain, high fever) and call your provider when unsure.

Frequently asked questions

When does morning sickness usually start and stop?

Nausea often begins around weeks 6–8 and eases for many people by weeks 12–14, as the first trimester ends. Some experience it longer, and a minority barely at all.

How much folic acid do I need?

Most guidelines recommend a daily prenatal vitamin containing folic acid before conception and through early pregnancy. Confirm the right amount for you with your healthcare provider, as some people need more.

Is light spotting normal in early pregnancy?

Light spotting can be common and often harmless, but heavy bleeding or bleeding with pain should be checked promptly. When in doubt, contact your provider.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
